research_text:
## Research brief — `java.security.spec.X509EncodedKeySpec`

### 1. Governed API and meaning of the reported event/value

`java.security.spec.X509EncodedKeySpec` is a **transparent public-key specification**. Oracle documents it as representing an ASN.1 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` encoding, the X.509-defined structure containing an `AlgorithmIdentifier` and a public-key bit string. It is therefore for an **encoded public key**, not a private-key encoding. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))

The applicable API event in the supplied CrySL rule is the **one-argument constructor event**, not an ordinary method call:

> `c1: X509EncodedKeySpec(encodedKey);`

The rule declares `encodedKey` as `byte[]`, so the written event is the one-argument `X509EncodedKeySpec(byte[])` constructor. That constructor’s Javadoc says the supplied array is assumed to contain an X.509-encoded key, and the constructor copies the array. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))

The detector phrase **“no preparation of the encoded key material was observed”** corresponds, in the rule text, to the sole prerequisite:

> `preparedKeyMaterial[encodedKey];`

The source provides **no definition** of `preparedKeyMaterial`, no producer event for it, and no runtime predicate or value test. Thus, from this rule alone, the report means only that the analysis did not establish that named predicate for the constructor argument. It does not document a JCA API property called “preparation,” nor does the rule itself establish a runtime fact about the byte array. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))

### 2. Officially documented usage and remediation

**Documented usage**

Oracle’s API documentation states:

- Supply an encoded **public key** that is assumed to be X.509 encoded; `null` causes `NullPointerException`. The constructor copies the input array to prevent later modification from changing the specification object. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))
- `getEncoded()` returns X.509-encoded key bytes and returns a **new array on each call**; `getFormat()` returns `"X.509"`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))
- A `KeyFactory` is the documented JCA conversion mechanism from a `KeySpec` to a `PublicKey`; `generatePublic(KeySpec)` creates a public key from the supplied specification and can throw `InvalidKeySpecException` when the specification is inappropriate for that factory. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html))
- The two-argument constructor accepts an algorithm name in addition to the encoded key. Oracle says it is useful when later callers of the specification may not otherwise know the key algorithm. The algorithm must be non-null and non-empty. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))

**What official sources do *not* document**

Neither the `X509EncodedKeySpec` nor `KeyFactory` documentation defines `preparedKeyMaterial`, specifies provenance or trust requirements for an encoded public key, or provides a prescribed remediation for a rule violation framed as “preparation was not observed.” The documented API behavior is format representation, defensive copying, and conversion through a suitable `KeyFactory`; it is not a documented input-trust or validation policy. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))

Accordingly, there is **no official-source-supported remediation recommendation for this specific predicate**. A review is required to identify what the rule author intended `preparedKeyMaterial` to mean; the supplied CrySL source does not say.

### 3. Compatibility, formats, platform support, and migration

**Persisted and wire-format semantics**

The documented byte representation is the X.509 public-key format: ASN.1 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo`. `X509EncodedKeySpec.getFormat()` returns `"X.509"`, and `getEncoded()` returns the X.509 encoding. Oracle’s `Key` documentation separately describes such standard key encodings as the external form used when a standard representation is needed outside the JVM, including transmission to another party. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))

The sources do **not** document a serialization or persistence-compatibility contract for serializing an `X509EncodedKeySpec` Java object itself. They document the encoded key bytes and their format, not an object-persistence migration mechanism. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))

**Platform-version support**

- `X509EncodedKeySpec` and its one-argument `byte[]` constructor are documented as available since **Java 1.2**. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))
- `X509EncodedKeySpec(byte[] encodedKey, String algorithm)` is documented as available since **Java 9**. Consequently, changing from the one-argument constructor to that overload is not compatible with Java runtimes before Java 9. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))

**Migration path**

The official API documentation does not provide a migration path for changing the byte encoding, changing storage or wire format, or satisfying the CrySL `preparedKeyMaterial` predicate. It describes both constructors as taking the encoded X.509 public key; the Java 9 overload additionally carries an algorithm name. It does not state a formal byte-for-byte compatibility guarantee, a conversion procedure, or a persistence migration plan. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/spec/X509EncodedKeySpec.html))

### 4. Exact matching rule in `X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl`

**Source:**  
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl

The file’s complete API-type and event declaration is:

```text
SPEC java.security.spec.X509EncodedKeySpec

OBJECTS
    byte[] encodedKey;

EVENTS
    c1: X509EncodedKeySpec(encodedKey);
    Con := c1;
```

The exact matching event clause is:

> `c1: X509EncodedKeySpec(encodedKey);`

The rule therefore states:

- **Receiver/API type:** `java.security.spec.X509EncodedKeySpec`, declared by the fully qualified `SPEC` line.
- **Matched member name:** no ordinary method is named. The only declared event is `X509EncodedKeySpec(encodedKey)`, i.e., a constructor-form event.
- **Parameter-list constraint:** yes. The event has exactly one declared argument, `encodedKey`, and the `OBJECTS` section declares that identifier as `byte[]`.
- **Condition/prerequisite:** the file’s `REQUIRES` section declares:

  > `preparedKeyMaterial[encodedKey];`

- **Postcondition:** it declares:

  > `speccedKey[this, _] after Con;`

  where `Con := c1`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))

**Namesake methods**

**No — not under the event written in this rule.** The rule declares a fully qualified governed type and a constructor-form event; it does not declare an event for an arbitrary method merely sharing the text `X509EncodedKeySpec`. The source contains no alternate event, wildcard, method-name-only pattern, or overload declaration. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))

**Source limitation:** the `.crysl` file does not describe the detector’s type-resolution, overload-resolution, or call-graph implementation. Therefore, while the rule text itself is scoped to `java.security.spec.X509EncodedKeySpec` and its sole declared event has one `byte[]` argument, the file alone cannot establish implementation-level guarantees about an external analyzer’s behavior if it mis-resolves types or calls. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/X509EncodedKeySpec.crysl))
